references.text: The Lord foretells that two nations shall come from Rebekah's womb, and that the older shall serve the younger—a prophecy pointing to the different characters of Esau and Jacob.
Isaac tells Esau to take his hunting gear and go out into the field to catch game—directly linked to Esau's description as a skilled hunter, a man of the field.
Jacob describes the contrast between himself and Esau: Esau is a hairy man, while Jacob is smooth-skinned—a reflection of their different natures.
Nimrod is described as a mighty hunter before the Lord, a parallel to Esau's description as a man who knew hunting (יֹדֵעַ צַיִד).
Job is described with the same Hebrew word 'tam' (תָּם, blameless/whole) that is used for Jacob—an important linguistic parallel.
The Letter to the Hebrews warns against being like Esau, who despised his birthright—a picture of his character as described in Gen 25:27.
Jabal is described as the ancestor of those who dwell in tents (יֹשֵׁב אֹהֶל), the same expression used for Jacob in 25:27.
The definition of character as 'a man of the field' (25:27) becomes the direct reason he is away when the blessing is to be given (27:5).
The contrast between Jacob's stillness and Esau's hunting is dramatically realized at the tent, where Esau returns home just as Jacob departs.
